en: The Sūtra of the Questions of the Devaputra Śreṣṭhī,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of North India during the Sui Dynasty.
At that time, the Bhagavat was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the great city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of...
The World-Honored One was accompanied by a multitude of one thousand two hundred and fifty people.

There was also a great assembly of Bodhisattvas, namely Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, and other leaders of the host, who had come together from various Buddha-fields beyond measure—both from the ten directions and from non-directional realms.
At that time, the Devaputra Sārthavāha, surrounded by a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas, came to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha's presence, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and made offerings to the Tathāgata with various kinds of ritual implements.
For the sake of hearing the Dharma, they were present before the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Prince of the Dharma.
At that time, the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will request Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Prince of the Dharma, to expound the essentials of the Dharma!"

Now, within this assembly there are various devaputras who have long been matured by Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Bodhisattva and Son of the Dharma King; once they have heard the wisdom and eloquence of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, they shall resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi!
"Having given rise to this mind, one attains non-retrogression within the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "Good son!"
"You should expound the essentials of the Dharma for the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta and for the other devas.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Son of the Dharma King, having received the Buddha’s instruction, addressed the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta, saying:
"You should listen with single-minded attention, receive it carefully, and reflect upon it well!"
I shall now analyze and explain this for you!

Just as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), reach the further shore regarding all phenomena (dharmas), swiftly fulfill the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā), and shall attain the practice of omniscience.
“O Son of Heaven!

All those who are wise Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas possess what are known as: the wisdom that knows suffering, the wisdom of bearing the burden of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the wisdom of accumulation, the wisdom of cultivating and gathering roots of goodness, the wisdom of cessation, the wisdom of origination, and the wisdom of the path.”
...the knowledge of non-path, the knowledge of causes, the knowledge of non-forgetting, the knowledge of results, the knowledge of the conditions for gathering and realizing all matters,
the knowledge of the abandonment of accumulations, the knowledge of reality, the knowledge of the Buddha, the knowledge of mastery, the knowledge of dependent origination,
the knowledge of manifesting through *avadāna*, the knowledge of the aggregates, the knowledge of removing desire and defilement, and the knowledge of the elements.
...the wisdom that shatters the dharma-realm, the wisdom of entry, the wisdom of contemplating the collection of emptiness, the wisdom of giving, the wisdom of not transgressing the proper time,
the wisdom of ethical discipline, the wisdom of maturing sentient beings who violate their precepts, the wisdom of patience, the wisdom of diligence,

the wisdom of skillfully performing all activities, the wisdom of meditative concentration, the wisdom of turning back from meditative concentration, the wisdom of insight, and the wisdom of vision...

The knowledge of knowing, the knowledge of skillful means, the knowledge of maturing sentient beings, the knowledge of loving-kindness, the knowledge of the vehicles of sentient beings, the knowledge of compassion,
the knowledge of being untiring, the knowledge of rejoicing, the knowledge of delighting in the Dharma with joyful love,
the knowledge of equanimity, the knowledge of accomplishing all Buddha-dharmas, the knowledge of delivering sentient beings, the knowledge of observation, and the constant upholding...

The knowledge of phenomena; the knowledge of causing [beings] to abide in what is not their proper sphere; the knowledge of right exertion; the knowledge of right awakening; the knowledge of the bases of supernormal power;
the knowledge of observing the non-constructive nature of all conditioned formations; the knowledge of the faculty and power of faith; the knowledge of transcending all wisdoms of wisdom;
the knowledge of the faculty and power of diligence; the knowledge of being unoppressed by any afflictions; mindfulness...
The wisdom of the faculties and powers; the wisdom that does not forget any phenomena; the wisdom of the faculties and powers of samādhi; the wisdom of the wisdom of the equality of all phenomena;
the wisdom of the faculties and powers; the wisdom of the preeminence of the faculties; the wisdom of the factors of enlightenment; the wisdom of realizing the path;
the wisdom of transcending all non-paths; the wisdom of focal objects; the wisdom of exhaustion; and all virtues.
The wisdom of the inexhaustibility of the faculties; the wisdom of the knowledge of non-arising; the wisdom of attaining the patient acceptance of the non-arising of all dharmas;

the wisdom of mindfulness of the Buddha; the wisdom of the accomplishment of one’s own body; the wisdom of mindfulness of the Dharma; the wisdom of turning the wheel of the Dharma; the wisdom of mindfulness of the Sangha;
the wisdom of entering the equality of the *abhibhū-samādhi*; the wisdom of mindfulness of giving; the wisdom of not abandoning any sentient beings; and mindfulness of...
The wisdom of ethical discipline (*śīla*); the wisdom of fulfilling all vows; the wisdom of mindfulness of non-existence; the wisdom of not committing any evil;

the wisdom of not conceptualizing phenomena; the wisdom of awakening to universal loving-kindness; the wisdom of fulfillment; the wisdom of never wearying of accomplishing all tasks; the wisdom that serves as medicine for all sentient beings;
the wisdom of skillful means in serving according to the Dharma; and the wisdom of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*).
The wisdom of non-action regarding what is impossible; the wisdom of the ten powers; the wisdom that accords with the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
the wisdom of fearlessness; the wisdom that awakens to all phenomena as being either obstructed or unobstructed;
the wisdom of non-attachment to past bodies; the wisdom of consciousness without dwelling; the wisdom of non-attachment to future bodies; and the wisdom that all phenomena do not proceed.
The wisdom that the present body is unattached; the wisdom that is neither fixed nor abiding; the wisdom that the body is supreme; the wisdom regarding all sentient beings;
the wisdom that enables them to cross over; the wisdom that takes speech as primary; the wisdom that discriminates the sounds of all sentient beings; the wisdom that takes the mind as primary;
the wisdom that knows the mental activities and inclinations of all sentient beings; and the wisdom that is free from error.

1. The wisdom that awakens all sentient beings from error; 2. The wisdom of what is pleasant and what is not pleasant; 3. The wisdom that extinguishes strife and contention; 4. The wisdom of right mindfulness that is never lost; 5.
The wisdom that causes sentient beings with distracted minds to abide in stability; 6. The wisdom that gathers samādhi; 7.
The wisdom of the uncommon Buddha-dharmas that gathers indolent sentient beings; 8. The wisdom of the timing for awakening those to be converted.
...the wisdom of skillful means, and the wisdom of prajñā.
O Son of Heaven!
These are the wisdoms of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; by means of such wisdoms as these, they shall attain the unimpeded great wisdom of all Buddhas.
At that time, the Devaputra Sārthavāha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Rare, rare indeed, Mañjuśrī!”
The wisdom of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the most preeminent within the three realms; it cannot be accomplished through minor adornments! Mañjuśrī!
If one can give rise to wisdom in this manner, that is a great supernormal power. Indeed, Mañjuśrī!
How does a bodhisattva become fully adorned?
He replied, “If all sentient beings possess the nature of nirvāṇa, they will not be terrified upon hearing it. He asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! For what reason is one called a bodhisattva? He replied:
“Son of Heaven!
Because he dwells in, maintains, and enters the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), he is called a bodhisattva. He asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! By what causes and conditions is one called a mahāsattva? He replied:
“Son of Heaven!
Because he has entered the Mahāyāna and because he has perfected great wisdom, he is called a Mahāsattva. He asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! By what causes and conditions is he named ‘Supreme Being’ (Sattva)? He replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
Because the Dharma-knowledge cannot be sought after in order to attain entry [into it], he is therefore named the Supreme Sattva. He asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! By what meaning is one called a ‘pure being’ (viśuddhasattva)? He replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
Because he does not dwell together with afflictions, and because he exerts diligence for the sake of extinguishing the afflictions of all sentient beings, he is called a Pure Being (Śuddhasattva).”
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
by what meaning is one called a 'Perfectly Pure Being' (viśuddhasattva)?"
He replied: "O Devaputra!
Because he causes all sentient beings to practice the path of purity, for this reason he is named 'Utterly Pure Being' (Suddhasattva)."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī! For what reason is one called a 'Guide' (śāstṛ)?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
Because, having established oneself in this path, one is able to bring immeasurable, incalculable sentient beings to maturity, one is therefore called a 'Guide'."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī! For what further reason is he called the 'Teacher of Discipline'?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
Because he tames sentient beings through ultimate non-contention, he is called the Great Master who Tames."
Again he asked: "Mañjuśrī,
how does a bodhisattva achieve valor and fortitude?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!

Because he subdues the various difficulties posed by Māras and hostile enemies, and subsequently undergoes existence to bring sentient beings to maturity, he is called a Bodhisattva who has achieved valor."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva cause others to rejoice?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
Having first made his vow and brought it to fulfillment, he does not rely on the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others; in this way, the bodhisattva causes others to rejoice."
Again, he asked: "Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva become supreme?"
He replied: "O Devaputra!

One should bring sentient beings to maturity through the skillful means of noble wisdom; by manifesting and clearly apprehending them within the True Dharma, a bodhisattva such as this attains the state of being supreme."
Again he asked: "Mañjuśrī,
how does a bodhisattva become one who turns the wheel of the Dharma?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
Relying on the Buddha’s authoritative speech, one cannot turn back from [the path of] all sentient beings; it is in this way that a bodhisattva attains the turning of the Dharma."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how should a bodhisattva practice transformative subduing?"
He replied: "O Devaputra!
A bodhisattva upholds the precepts and abides in the precepts, extinguishing all nets of doubt belonging to sentient beings; such a bodhisattva is said to be 'transformed and tamed.'"
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how does a bodhisattva attain the turning of meaning?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
To practice according to what one has heard and to truly bestow it upon others—such a bodhisattva is said to be 'one who turns the meaning.'"
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how does a bodhisattva accomplish the benefit of all sentient beings?"
He replied: "O Devaputra!
By dedicating all the virtues one has cultivated toward sentient beings, a bodhisattva thus accomplishes benefit."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how is it that a bodhisattva is able to cultivate a straightforward mind?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one has committed an offense oneself and does not conceal it, such a bodhisattva shall attain a straightforward mind."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī, how should a bodhisattva cultivate a correct mind?"
He replied: "Devaputra!
If there are sentient beings who possess desire, hatred, and delusion, yet one does not feel anger or reproach toward them, such a bodhisattva is said to have a 'right mind'."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī, how should a bodhisattva practice without guile?"
He replied: "Devaputra!
As it is said and as it is practiced, in this way a bodhisattva shall attain freedom from deceit."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how is it that a bodhisattva does not create illusions?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
As it is with what the mind conceives, so it is with what the mouth speaks; in this way, such a bodhisattva is said to be without illusion."
He asked again: “Mañjuśrī,
how does a bodhisattva attain a mind free from pride?”
He replied, “Devaputra!
When one bows with palms joined toward all sentient beings, one does not commit evil; in this way, a bodhisattva attains a mind free from pride.”
Again, he asked: "Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva act as a great donor?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one can accomplish the great relinquishment of awakening (bodhi-mahātyāga), how much more so other things? Such a bodhisattva is called a great donor."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how does a bodhisattva come to be named 'one who upholds the precepts'?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one sees a violation of the precepts and yet, even for the sake of one's life, does not abandon the bodhicitta—such a bodhisattva is said to be one who upholds the precepts."
Again, he asked: "Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva accomplish patience?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one endures being oppressed oneself without oppressing others, such a bodhisattva accomplishes patience."
Again, he asked: "Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva exert diligent effort?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one discerns all phenomena and finds no phenomenon that can be apprehended, such a bodhisattva is said to have aroused diligent vigor."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how does a bodhisattva come to be named 'one who possesses meditative concentration'?"
He replied, “Devaputra!
If one can manifest rebirth within the desire realm, such a bodhisattva is said to have attained meditative concentration.”
Again, he asked: "Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva accomplish prajñā?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one does not perform the activities of prajñā, it is in this way that a bodhisattva accomplishes prajñā."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how should a bodhisattva practice a mind of loving-kindness?"
He replied: "Devaputra!
If one can contemplate that the realm of sentient beings is empty, such a bodhisattva is said to practice the mind of loving-kindness."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī, how should a bodhisattva practice compassion?"
He replied, “O Son of Heaven!
If one knows that all phenomena and awakening are like empty space, yet does not abandon diligent effort, such a bodhisattva is said to have accomplished the mind of compassion.”
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how should a bodhisattva practice the mind of sympathetic joy?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one attains both silence and tranquility, yet delights in seeking all dharmas without ever being satisfied—such a bodhisattva is called 'one who knows contentment.'"
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how is it that a bodhisattva is able to practice the mind of equanimity?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one is not submerged by the world, but acts within the world to rescue the world, such a bodhisattva is able to accomplish the mind of equanimity."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva attain a pure body?"
He replied: "O Devaputra!
If one manifests to sentient beings a body of equality through a phantom-like transformation body, it is in this way that a bodhisattva can attain a purified body."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva attain a pure mouth?"
He replied, “Devaputra!
If one can provide all sentient beings with a perfect voice to expound the essentials of the Dharma without any fault or affliction, such a bodhisattva is able to purify their verbal karma.”
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how is it that a bodhisattva is able to purify the mind?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one knows that all minds are but a single mind, such a bodhisattva is said to have attained a pure mind."
Again, he asked: "Mañjuśrī, how can a bodhisattva obtain the divine eye?"
He replied: "Devaputra!

One who perceives all forms and figures should remain detached from all forms; by constantly contemplating all forms and remaining far removed from them, such a bodhisattva is said to have attained the divine eye."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how is it that a bodhisattva is said to have attained the divine ear?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one hears various sounds, one should contemplate those sounds as being devoid of the characteristics of sound; a bodhisattva who acts thus is said to have attained the divine ear."
Again, he asked: "Mañjuśrī,
how is it that a bodhisattva is able to know the minds of others?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one knows the flow and succession of mental formations, their arising and ceasing, then such a bodhisattva is able to know the minds of others."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how is it that a bodhisattva is able to know his past lives?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one contemplates the original limit as being identical to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and does not increase [conceptual proliferation], such a bodhisattva is able to know past lives."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
how is it that a bodhisattva is able to attain the supernormal powers?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one can manifest various illusions yet remain unstained by the karma of illusion, such a bodhisattva is said to have attained supernormal powers."
Again, he asked: "Mañjuśrī! How does a bodhisattva become vast?"
He replied: “O Son of Heaven!
One should transform boundless sentient beings; it is in this way that a bodhisattva is said to have attained greatness.”
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī,
in what way is a bodhisattva to be called one who walks alone?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If one does not dwell together with the sense faculties, such a bodhisattva is said to be 'walking alone.'"
He asked again: “Mañjuśrī,
how is it that a bodhisattva is able to perform subduing?”
He replied, “Devaputra!
Because he has attained the dharma of being unshakable and free from anger, such a bodhisattva is said to have attained subduing.”
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī, how can a bodhisattva attain tranquility?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!

If one remains amidst afflictions yet is not burned by those various evil afflictions, and preaches the Dharma for the sake of extinguishing the afflictions of all sentient beings—such a bodhisattva is said to have attained tranquility."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī, how can a bodhisattva attain faith?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
If even when the Buddha-body is broken, it cannot be destroyed, such a bodhisattva shall attain faith."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva employ skillful means?"
He replied, “Devaputra!
If one perceives that awakening is shared with all sentient beings, such a bodhisattva is said to possess skillful means.”

At that time, as Mañjuśrī was preaching this Dharma, twelve thousand beings among the great assembly resolved their minds toward Bodhicitta, and five hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
Excellent, excellent!”
"You have well expounded this Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas. It is so, it is so!
You have been able to speak of such great merits for those sublime beings; furthermore, there are immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas more."
At that time, the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta again asked the Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva: "Mañjuśrī!
To how many Buddhas did you make offerings in the past to obtain such eloquence as this?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
It is like a magically conjured person whose mental activity ceases."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī!
Even an emanation has no thought; how much more so that which is not an emanation?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
Such is the essential nature and form of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas; they are to be honored and served with such characteristics."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī! At what time do you practice the dānapāramitā?"
He replied: "Devaputra! If they have been emanated by the Tathāgata."
Again, he asked: "I previously asked you:
'At what time did you practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)?'"
"Why do you now give such an answer? He replied, "O Devaputra!"
"He had no answer; my response was as follows.
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
"If the characteristics of a transformation are thus, how should one answer me regarding the practice of the *dānapāramitā* at that time?"
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī! As I reflect upon it, are you perhaps stingy?"
He replied, “Devaputra! I am indeed stingy.”
He asked again: "By what causes and conditions do you speak thus? He replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
If the mind does not relinquish, this is called stinginess. He asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! How is it that not relinquishing [anything] is called ‘miserliness’? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! I never abandon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, nor do I abandon any sentient beings.
For this reason, I am said to be stingy.”
Again he asked: "According to my reflection upon what Mañjuśrī has said, you too have now broken the precepts! He replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
I too have violated the precepts. He asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! For what reason do you speak thus? He replied:
“Devaputra! If a person violates the precepts, will they not surely fall into the three evil realms?
The Devaputra replied:
"It is truly as the holy teaching says! Mañjuśrī said,
"O Devaputra!..."
"I intentionally contemplate falling into the evil realms in order to bring sentient beings to maturity.
For this reason, I am called one who has broken the precepts.
He was asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! Do you not possess a mind of anger? Mañjuśrī replied:
"So it is, O Devaputra! He asked again:
"By what causes and conditions do you speak thus?"
Mañjuśrī asked: "Is it not the case that one who possesses a mind of anger has no affection? He replied:
"So it is! Mañjuśrī said. "Therefore, O Devaputra!..."
"I have no affection for afflictions, nor for Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
For this reason, I harbor a mind of anger. He asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! Do you now have any mind of indolence? He replied:
"So it is! He asked again: "Mañjuśrī!
"For what reason do you speak thus?
He replied, "O Devaputra!"
Now, one who is indolent does not initiate the cultivation of various practices through body, speech, or mind.
I am now like this: neither do I abandon practice, nor do I desire to practice; I neither relinquish nor grasp.
"For this reason, I am called 'the indolent. He asked again: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"Do you perhaps still have a distracted mind? He replied, "It is so!"
He asked again: "By what causes and conditions do you speak thus? He replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
One who is indolent has no place of abiding; that too is said to be a distracted mind.
O Son of Heaven!”
Among the noble ones, my mind has attained liberation; because I bring all sentient beings to maturity, I have no fixed abode.
For this reason, I am called "the distracted one."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī! Do you not possess wisdom at this time?"
He replied, “It is so, O Devaputra! He asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! For what reason do you speak in this way? He replied:
“Devaputra! Is it not because you lack wisdom that you do not fear birth and death, do not dread the afflictions, and instead enjoy yourself in the company of deluded sentient beings?”
He replied, “It is so, Mañjuśrī! Mañjuśrī spoke again:

“Devaputra! Within birth-and-death and amidst all afflictions, I feel neither fear nor terror. I dwell together with deluded sentient beings, sharing in their pleasures for the sake of bringing them to maturity; therefore, they say that I possess no wisdom.”
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī! Could it be that you are not a field of merit for the world?"
He replied: "O Devaputra!
Because it constitutes the destruction of a field of merit."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī! For what reason do you speak thus?"
He replied: "O Devaputra!
Those who ought to be slain are desire, hatred, and delusion."
"If one can slay that [person], this is indeed a great field of merit! He asked again: "Mañjuśrī!..."
“Worldly beings, upon hearing what you have said, will for the most part give rise to fear!
He replied, “O Devaputra!
If there is fear regarding the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), then the world likewise gives rise to fear. Why is this?
Because the entire world does not depart from the limit of reality; it abides within the limit of reality.
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī! If there were someone who disparaged what you have said, where would that person go?"
He replied: “Devaputra! One should head toward nirvāṇa!”
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī! For what reason do you speak thus?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
There is nothing whatsoever that, without destroying its own verbal expression, can reach the noble liberation."
Why is this? Because within the Noble Path there are no names, phrases, or words that can be spoken or demonstrated.
Those who do not believe shall not attain liberation!
He asked again: “Mañjuśrī! For what reason do you speak thus?”
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
It is not possible for one who has already attained liberation to attain liberation again."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī!
Does one who slanders the true Dharma not fall into hell?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
As for liberation, it is entirely free from dust."
Again, he asked: "Mañjuśrī!
The Dharma you have taught provides no assistance whatsoever."
He replied: "Devaputra!
One cannot provide assistance within emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."
Again he asked: "Mañjuśrī! What should one who practices emptiness practice?"
He replied, "Devaputra!
One who practices emptiness is precisely one who practices loving-kindness toward all sentient beings."
Why is this so? It is because emptiness is not separate from all sentient beings. He asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! How does a bodhisattva reach the limit regarding all sentient beings? He replied:
“O Son of Heaven!

If one perceives that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, and furthermore does not fall into the views of nihilism or eternalism—for this reason, a bodhisattva is said to have reached the limit of sentient beings.”
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī! What realm is the realm of sentient beings?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
The dharma-realm is the realm of sentient beings."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, what realm is the Dharma-realm?"
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
The nature and realm of space is the Dharma-realm."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, what kind of realm is this realm of empty space?"
He replied: "O Devaputra!
That which transcends all spheres is the realm of empty space."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī! What kind of realm is that Buddha-realm?"
He replied: "Devaputra!
The realm of the eye is the realm of the Buddha; yet that realm of the Buddha is likewise not the realm of the eye, form, or consciousness."
The realm of the ear is itself the Buddha-realm; yet that Buddha-realm is likewise not the realm of the ear, sound, or auditory consciousness.
The realm of the nose is the Buddha-realm; yet that Buddha-realm is likewise not the realm of the nose, fragrance, or olfactory consciousness.
The realm of the tongue is the Buddha-realm; yet that Buddha-realm is likewise not the realm of the tongue, flavor, or gustatory consciousness.
The realm of the body is the realm of the Buddha, yet that realm of the Buddha is likewise not the realm of body, touch, or consciousness;
the realm of the mind is the realm of the Buddha, yet that realm of the Buddha is likewise not the realm of mind, phenomena, or consciousness;
the realm of form is the realm of the Buddha, yet that realm of the Buddha is likewise not the realm of form.
The realm of sensation is the Buddha-realm, yet that Buddha-realm is not a realm of sensation;
the realm of perception is the Buddha-realm, yet that Buddha-realm does not contemplate realms;
the realm of volitional formations is the Buddha-realm, yet that Buddha-realm is likewise an unconditioned realm.
The realm of the various consciousnesses is the realm of the Buddha; yet that realm of the Buddha is likewise not a realm of cognitive apprehension.
The realm of ignorance is the realm of the Buddha; yet that realm of the Buddha is likewise not a realm of causes and conditions.
Even so, the realm of old age and death is the realm of the Buddha; yet that realm of the Buddha does not undergo the realms of those states.
The realm of desire is the realm of the Buddha, yet that realm of the Buddha is also not a realm of desire;
the realm of form is the realm of the Buddha, yet that realm of the Buddha is also not a realm of form;
the realm of formlessness is the realm of the Buddha, yet that realm of the Buddha is also not a realm of the visible world.
The realm of the conditioned is the Buddha-realm, yet that Buddha-realm is not a dualistic realm;
the realm of the unconditioned is the Buddha-realm, yet that Buddha-realm likewise does not depart from the realm of the three marks.
"O Son of Heaven!
This is the realm of all Buddhas.
Whatever realm there may be—the entry into all realms, the boundless realm—this is the realm of the Buddha."
“Devaputra! Once a bodhisattva mahāsattva has entered this realm, they act within the sphere of benefiting all sentient beings and do not give rise to the realm of Māra.”
One should realize that the realm of Māra and the realm of the Buddha are equal and non-dual, not to be treated as separate realms.
O Devaputra!
This is the great wisdom and supernormal power of a bodhisattva; if one can transcend the realm of equality, one brings sentient beings to maturity by means of that realm of equality.
“Devaputra! In this regard, what is equality and what is inequality?”
Because all phenomena are equal in their emptiness;
if a bodhisattva does not enter into this equality of emptiness, that person abides in inequality.
Nevertheless, while maturing those beings, the bodhisattva remains unmoved within the dharma of emptiness.
All dharmas are equal because they are without marks;
if a bodhisattva does not enter into this equality of marklessness, that person dwells in inequality.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these [qualities], they do not waver even within the dharma of marklessness.
All phenomena are equal because they are wishless;
if a bodhisattva does not enter into this equality of wishlessness, that person dwells in inequality.
The bodhisattva brings them to maturity, yet remains unmoved within the dharma of wishlessness.
All phenomena are equal because they are unconditioned;
if a bodhisattva does not enter into this equality of the unconditioned, that person abides in inequality.
The bodhisattva brings that equality to maturity, yet remains unmoved within the state of the unconditioned.
All dharmas are equal because they are equal in being neither born nor emerging;
they are equal because they are equal in being free from desire and solitary;
they are equal because they are equal in nirvana, wherein nothing can be extinguished.
If a bodhisattva does not enter this equality, that person dwells in inequality;
yet, even as the bodhisattva brings them to maturity, he does not move from within the dharma of nirvāṇa.
“O Son of Heaven!
When a bodhisattva enters into such practice that is both equal and unequal, this is what is called ‘practicing the bodhisattva path.
At that time, the Son of Heaven Śreṣṭhidatta again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying these words:
“Mañjuśrī! You should now explain what constitutes the practice of a bodhisattva. Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
The practice of a bodhisattva is inconceivable. He asked again:
“What is the inconceivable practice of a bodhisattva? He replied, “O Devaputra!
Because desire is inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice is likewise not separate from the practice of desire.
Because the practice of hatred is inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice is likewise not separate from the practice of hatred.
Because the practice of folly is inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice likewise constitutes the practice of prajñā.
The practice of non-envy is the bodhisattva’s practice, nor does it involve the thought of practicing giving.
To remain far removed from the practice of breaking the precepts is the bodhisattva practice, yet one does not dwell upon the practice of the precepts.
To remain free from anger is the bodhisattva practice, yet one does not dwell upon the practice of patience.
To practice without indolence is the bodhisattva practice, yet one does not even dwell on the practice of diligence.
To practice without distraction is the bodhisattva practice, yet one does not even dwell on the practice of meditative concentration.
The practice of non-wisdom is not the bodhisattva practice, nor does one dwell upon the practice of prajñā.
The practice of non-affliction is the bodhisattva practice, nor does one dwell upon the practice of freedom from affliction.
The practice of non-compassion is the bodhisattva’s practice, because of giving internal things.
The practice of non-pity is the bodhisattva’s practice, because of giving away sons, daughters, wives, and children.
The practice of non-delight is the bodhisattva’s practice, because of never being weary of the merits of all desires.
The practice of never being angry is the bodhisattva practice, because it gathers all roots of goodness.
The practice of not abandoning is the bodhisattva practice, because it relinquishes body and life.
The practice of non-attachment is the bodhisattva practice, because it relinquishes both hatred and love.
The practice of fearlessness is the bodhisattva practice, because it does not draw near to the activities of birth-and-death or afflictions.
The practice of bearing great responsibility is the bodhisattva practice, for it involves taking up the heavy burden of all sentient beings.
The practice of non-oppression is the bodhisattva practice, for it arises from the vow made in the past to deliver them.
The practice of non-regret is the bodhisattva practice, because it is free from withdrawal or remorse.
The supreme practice is the bodhisattva practice, because it is the most excellent among all that is superior.
The adamantine armor practice is the bodhisattva practice, because one firmly establishes vows without deficiency or diminution.
The practice of the extinction of one’s own mind is the bodhisattva practice, because the minds of all sentient beings are extinguished.
The practice of non-loss is the bodhisattva practice, because the karma performed is not lost.
The practice of non-conceptualization is the bodhisattva’s practice, because of the mind of equality toward all sentient beings.
The practice of valor is the bodhisattva’s practice, because of the subduing of enemies.
The practice free from admixture is the bodhisattva’s practice, because it accords with the cultivation of meditative concentration through spiritual friends.
The practice of joy is the bodhisattva’s practice, because it causes all who are evil to rejoice.
The practice of joyful exultation is the bodhisattva practice, because of the joy felt upon seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and serving the Honored Ones.
The practice of adornment is the bodhisattva practice, because of the adornment of the buddha-fields through body, speech, and mind.
The practice of being unsubdued is the bodhisattva practice, because it provides impartial benefit and assistance.
The practice of non-slander is the bodhisattva practice, because it is praised by the wise.
The practice of non-oppression is the bodhisattva practice, for it correctly contemplates all afflictions.
The practice of the virtuous man is the bodhisattva practice, for it bears the heavy burden to reach the other shore.
The practice of benefiting others is the bodhisattva’s practice, because it is characterized by firm diligence and lack of indolence or retreat.
The practice of the Dharma is the bodhisattva’s practice, because it involves the thorough cultivation of all dharmas that assist the path.
The practice of knowing and repaying kindness is the bodhisattva practice, because it ensures that the lineage of all Buddhas is never severed.
The practice of precious jewels is the bodhisattva practice, because it extols and proclaims the Triple Gem.
"The practice of wisdom and skillful means is the bodhisattva practice, because it does not sever the various means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).

When this bodhisattva practice was being taught, five hundred bodhisattvas entered the bodhisattva practice and attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
At that time, the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Mañjuśrī! You have skillfully explained these practices of the bodhisattvas."
"If there are bodhisattvas who do not depart from this practice, I shall bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta, saying: "So it is, so it is, devaputra!"
"It is as you have said, O Devaputra!

In the past, I did not depart from this practice, and the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara then bestowed upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; at that time, I immediately attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."
“O Son of Heaven!
This is the great wisdom-practice of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
At that time, the Son of Heaven Śreṣṭhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘non-arising’?
In relation to what phenomena, and within what phenomena, does one attain non-arising?”
He replied: "O Son of Heaven!
That which is unarisen is fundamentally and inherently unborn."
The characteristic of the limit is the meaning of non-arising.
That which did not arise previously does not arise subsequently either.
Yet, as for that non-arising, it has fundamentally no place of arising.
However, that which has come from before has no place from which it emerged, nor does it emerge later.
Its intrinsic nature is fundamentally such that there is no place of birth.
For this reason, it was not produced from any location in the past, nor will it be produced from any location at a later time.
The self-nature is primordial and has no place of origin.
Since it was never created in the past, it cannot be created later either;
for the self-nature is by nature unconditioned.
Since it did not exist previously, it likewise does not exist subsequently; it is ultimately non-existent.
It was never included among the category of *pudgala* from the outset, and therefore it is not included in that category subsequently either, because its intrinsic nature is empty.

Since those phenomena had no characteristics that could be described or demonstrated previously, they likewise have no characteristics that can be described or demonstrated later; for those phenomena were originally without characteristics.
If a person awakens in this manner, they do not even give rise to a mind that seeks to shatter their own realization through grasping.
For this reason, it is called "non-arising.
What is meant by "patience" (kṣānti)?
Thus, being unborn and thus enduring all sentient beings is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Thus, being unborn and thus enduring all lands is called patience.
This non-arising can be endured regarding all those in training, those beyond training, and pratyekabuddhas; therefore, it is called patience (*kṣānti*).
This non-arising can be endured regarding all Buddha-dharmas, all bodhisattva practices, and all Buddhas; therefore, it is called patience.
Thus, because there is no arising, one is able to endure all phenomena in this way; therefore, it is called "patience" (kṣānti).
Now, as for that which is non-existent, why is it called "non-existent"?
It is non-existent because there is no non-existence.
Because it is empty of emptiness, it is non-existent;
because it is signless of signlessness, it is non-existent;
as with emptiness and signlessness, because it is the characteristic of emptiness, it is non-existent.
If a dharma is non-existent, it lacks sovereignty;
if there is no sovereignty, there is no desire;
if there is no desire, that is the true nature.
If it is true nature, it is called "naturelessness.
All phenomena are non-existent; they are empty, devoid of self-mastery, and far removed from falsehood.
If one possesses such patience regarding all phenomena, this is called "patience"; yet even this patience does not exist. Because patience does not exist, there is therefore no self.

"In this state of equality, a bodhisattva shall receive the prediction of enlightenment and realize the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); yet, that dharma of patience cannot be apprehended!
What is the meaning of 'realizing' within this?"
Whether it be "I" or "patience," these two are acquisitions; this is called acquisition.
Whether it be a "sentient being," a "life-force," a "nourished person" (*pudgala*), "patience," or "omniscience," these are called acquisitions.
What is the true patience of non-attainment regarding intrinsic nature?
It is the patience toward that true nature wherein, within this meaning, one does not grasp at subject or object; the dual capacity to realize and enter [this state] is called "non-attainment."
Briefly stated, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena—the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—is called emptiness.
That which is emptiness is the unconditioned.
Just as the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is such, so too is the nature of all that is created.
If one does not perceive agent or object within this fundamental nature, such realization and knowledge is called "non-attainment" (*anupalambha*).
"O Son of Heaven!

Thus, when one is fully endowed with the perfection of patience, a bodhisattva mahāsattva may practice this conduct of patience for as many as incalculable eons (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa); this is the bodhisattva’s path of great wisdom and power!"

When this patience was preached, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; a brilliant light filled all worlds; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; and great clouds of flowers rained down.

Forty thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and ninety-six thousand sentient beings attained the *anulomikī-kṣānti*. By the power of the Buddha and the power of the Dharma, this entire world was made to appear exactly as it had been in the past when the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara entered the Lotus City, manifesting just as it originally did.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled. As is the custom of all Buddhas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rays of light of various colors issued from the Buddha’s mouth—namely blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and crystal-colored—and reached immeasurable and boundless worlds.
Having illuminated them all, it returned and circled the World-Honored One three times before re-entering the crown of the Buddha’s head.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, asked the World-Honored One in accordance with the Dharma and its meaning:
“I ask the World-Honored One of incomparable virtue; I ask the World-Honored One of majestic radiance.”
I ask: why does the Muni manifest a smile, now that he has cast off the cataracts of affliction?
I ask the World-Honored One who has subdued the heterodox; I ask the World-Honored One who has severed the power of Māra;
I ask the World-Honored One, the possessor of the ten powers—by what cause does the Muni manifest a smile?
I ask the World-Honored One about your extraordinary form, adorned with the wondrous majesty of the thirty-two marks;
since your virtuous conduct brings such great joy, for what reason, O Honored One, do you now manifest a smile?
I ask the Wisdom-Pool and the Wisdom-Tree, who have received the wisdom to instruct the world and manifest the boundless dharmas of wisdom: for what reason, World-Honored One, do you now smile?
The fame of the Three Realms has already spread; you have increased the Threefold Knowledge and uprooted the three defilements.
Having crossed over to the Three Liberations, O Lord of the Three Realms, for what reason do you now manifest a smile?
As the supreme physician for the ultimate end of old age and death, O Honored One with webbed fingers and wheels upon your hands and feet,
whose body is like that of the invincible Nārāyaṇa, O Muni, please explain the cause for emitting this light.
Who now practices pure conduct therein?
Who today fulfills all the perfections of patience?
Who shall have correct faith in the virtues of the Buddhas?
For this reason, the Muni now smiles;
it is not without cause that the Honored One of incomparable body, the Guide of virtuous conduct, manifests this light.
How excellent! We pray that you will proclaim the Buddha’s voice, so that sentient beings, upon hearing it, may give rise to joy.
When Ānanda had spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the venerable Ānanda, saying: “Ānanda,
while this *dharmaparyāya-sūtra* was being taught, seventy-two thousand sentient beings among this assembly gave rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
Furthermore, thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. Ānanda!
Do you see this Devaputra, the Merchant Leader?
He replied, "I have seen them, Blessed One!"
"I have seen it,
Sugata! The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda, saying:
“Ānanda! This Devaputra Śreṣṭhī, in the past, has already made offerings to Buddhas beyond calculation, serving and honoring them, inquiring about their meaning, and exhorting them [to teach].”
Furthermore, he exhorted immeasurable sentient beings to practice for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, causing them to abide therein as they should. Ānanda!

After two *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed, this Devaputra Śreṣṭhin will realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and appear in the world as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Guṇarājaprabhāsa.
That world is named Pure, and its eon is named Stainless.
"Ānanda! That Pure World is composed of the seven treasures, namely: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, amber, and red pearls."
At that time, that buddha-field was as level as the palm of a hand, adorned with eightfold paths and covered by hanging nets of jewels.

Within that buddha-field, there were no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor were there any non-Buddhists such as Carakas or Parivrājakas; there were no māras, nor were there any who committed the five heinous crimes, nor any who slandered the Buddha’s true Dharma.
That buddha-field is free from the eight difficulties; food and drink appear according to whatever one thinks of, and even the names of suffering or the violation of precepts do not exist there.
Those sentient beings experience the retribution of bliss, just like those in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).

The bodies of all those sentient beings are golden in color and they are fully endowed with the thirty-two marks; for the most part, they abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and for this reason that world is named "Pure."
The lifespan of that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Guṇarājaprabhāsa, was one thousand and forty kalpas.
By the power of their vows, the multitude of bodhisattvas in that buddha-land relinquish their life-span at will during that interval.
At that time, that Tathāgata had an assembly of six billion two hundred million great bodhisattvas.

“Ānanda! Now, there are bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); all of them shall attain rebirth in a pure buddha-field, within the realm of that Tathāgata Guṇarājaprabhāsa.”
At that time, that Tathāgata bestowed upon them all the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Then, among the assembly, there was a devaputra named Āśvāsaka who, sitting within the gathering, scattered heavenly māndārava flowers over the Tathāgata and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."

When that World-Honored One, King of Merit and Radiance, realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may I become a universal monarch (cakravartin) in that pure world to make offerings to that Buddha and the assembly of bodhisattvas!
"May I, immediately after that Buddha, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda!..."

When that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Guṇarājaprabhāsa, realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this Ānāpānasmṛti-deva was a universal monarch (cakravartin) in that world named Sudarśana; he made offerings to that Tathāgata with immeasurable and boundless varieties of requisites, fully perfecting the dharmas that assist awakening.
That Blessed One later appeared in the world, realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and was named Samantaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Ānanda! After King Sudarśana had performed the consecration of the crown prince, at one time, within that Buddha’s teaching, he developed faith, renounced his home, and left the household life to study the Path.
At that time, when that Tathāgata was approaching parinirvāṇa, he bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon that bodhisattva and then entered parinirvāṇa, speaking these words:
"This Bodhisattva Sudarśana shall, after me, realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening!"
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Devaputra Śreṣṭhin, saying:
"Devaputra! The Tathāgata has already bestowed upon you the prediction of enlightenment."
He replied: "Venerable Śāriputra!

The Buddha has granted me a prediction, just as a person created by a Tathāgata through transformation receives a prediction. It is like this suchness (tathatā) now; in a future age, it will return to this same suchness, yet this suchness neither increases nor decreases."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying: “Ānanda!
You should receive this Dharma-text, uphold it, explain it, read it, and recite it; you should apply yourself to its cultivation and expound it extensively for others.”

For the sake of the vast benefit of many people, for the sake of the peace and happiness of many people, and for the sake of extensively gathering in and benefiting the peace and happiness of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the present and future.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have already received this Dharma-text.”
"Bhagavān! What is the name of this dharma-text? How shall we uphold it?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This Dharma-text is titled 'Abhijñopadeśa' (Instruction on Supernormal Knowledges); you should uphold it thus.
This Dharma-text was spoken by the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī; you should receive and uphold it thus."
It is also titled "The Questions of the Devaputra Sārthavāha"; thus should it be upheld!

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda and the other bhikṣus, the Devaputra Sārthavāha and countless, boundless, asaṃkhyeya koṭis and nayutas of other devaputras, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and countless other asaṃkhyeya bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gathered from various worlds throughout the ten directions, as well as all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, humans, non-humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra of the Questions of the Devaputra Śreṣṭhināyaka (The Scripture on the Questions of the Heavenly Son Lord of Merchants)
